lead: This unit explains the semiconductor switches of power electronics: power diodes, thyristors and their relatives (TRIAC, DIAC, GTO), power BJTs, MOSFETs and IGBTs, and the new SiC and GaN devices. After it you can read a device datasheet, choose a switch for a converter, design its trigger or gate drive and snubber, and work out its losses and heat sink.
about: The unit starts with the power diode, the switch with no control terminal, and builds the thyristor from four layers: its V–I curve, the two-transistor model, how it is triggered and how commutation turns it off. TRIAC, DIAC and GTO extend the thyristor to AC switching and gate turn-off. The fully controlled transistors (BJT, MOSFET and IGBT) follow, with the MOSFET's switching intervals. The last chapters protect and cool these devices (ratings, snubbers, gate drives, switching loss and heat sinks) and end with SiC and GaN.

chapters.idea: A power diode is a two-terminal switch whose static curve shows forward drop and reverse leakage, and whose turn-off is limited by reverse recovery.
chapters.depth: Cover PN junction structure, forward and reverse bias, static V-I curve with cut-in voltage and reverse saturation current. State ideal switch requirements: zero on-state voltage, infinite off-state resistance, zero switching time and no loss; then compare with a real diode. Define forward recovery time, reverse recovery time t_rr, peak reverse recovery current I_RRM, reverse recovery charge Q_rr and softness factor. Explain dynamic turn-on and turn-off waveforms. Mention diode types by name only (standard, fast-recovery, Schottky). A one-line map of converter types (rectifier, chopper, inverter, AC controller) can be given, but circuits belong to Units 2–5.

figure.aria: Diode current stays at 10 A until 2 μs, falls to a peak reverse value of −8 A at 2.2 μs, and recovers to zero at 4 μs.

chapters.example: A diode carries 10 A. Its reverse recovery time is 2 μs and peak reverse recovery current is 8 A. Treat the recovery charge as a triangle and find Q_rr. If the diode blocks 300 V and switches at 20 kHz, find the average reverse-recovery power loss using P_rr = Q_rr V_s f_s. Answer: Q_rr = 0.5 × 8 A × 2 μs = 8 μC; P_rr = 8 μC × 300 V × 20 kHz = 48 W.
chapters.trap: Do not add t_rr to t_on; reverse recovery is a turn-off effect, and Q_rr is charge, not current.
chapters.prereq: Basic PN junction diode from semiconductor devices.
chapters.leave: Rectifier circuits and filter design go to Unit 2; diode types for SMPS go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An SCR is a four-layer PNPN latch that turns on when gate current makes the two internal transistors regenerate.
chapters.depth: Draw the four layers P-N-P-N, anode, cathode and gate. Explain forward blocking, forward conduction, reverse blocking, latching current I_L, holding current I_H and breakover voltage V_BO. Derive the two-transistor model with current gains α1 and α2; state turn-on when α1+α2 approaches 1. Cover gate characteristics and ratings only as needed. Some syllabi call the SCR a silicon controlled rectifier or thyristor; use both names.

figure.title: Two-transistor model
figure.aria: Anode current enters a PNP transistor, its collector drives an NPN transistor, and the NPN collector feeds back to the PNP base; gate current starts the loop.

chapters.example: In the two-transistor model of an SCR, α1 = 0.6 and α2 = 0.3. Find α1 + α2. Can the SCR stay on after the gate pulse? Repeat if α2 rises to 0.45. Answer: 0.9, no; 1.05, yes.
chapters.trap: Gate current only starts conduction; it cannot turn off an SCR. Latching current is larger than holding current, and both are not gate ratings.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for diode blocking and conduction ideas; basic transistor current gain α.
chapters.leave: Gate trigger circuits go to 1.3; turn-off methods go to 1.4; series/parallel operation and protection go to 1.7.

chapters.idea: A thyristor turns on by gate, thermal, light or overvoltage, and a gate trigger circuit must supply a fast pulse with enough current and voltage.
chapters.depth: List turn-on methods: gate, thermal, light, forward-voltage breakover and dv/dt. Explain gate-cathode characteristics, gate pulse width, rise time and latching current. Draw R triggering, RC triggering, UJT relaxation oscillator and pulse-transformer isolation. Define gate trigger voltage V_GT and gate trigger current I_GT. Some syllabi call the UJT circuit a relaxation oscillator.

figure.title: Gate trigger path
figure.aria: A control pulse and a 12 V source feed a 105 Ω series resistor, which drives the SCR gate-cathode path.

chapters.example: A 12 V trigger source drives an SCR gate with V_GT = 1.5 V and I_GT = 100 mA. Find the series gate resistance R_s and its power loss. Use R_s = (V_s − V_GT)/I_GT. Answer: R_s = (12 − 1.5)/0.1 = 105 Ω; P = I²R_s = 1.05 W.
chapters.trap: A gate resistor must be rated for pulse power; do not use the DC gate current rating as an average. The gate pulse should be removed after latching.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for thyristor structure and latching current.
chapters.leave: Commutation and forced turn-off go to 1.4; snubber dv/dt protection goes to 1.7.

chapters.idea: Commutation is the process of reducing anode current below holding current and allowing the SCR to regain forward blocking.
chapters.depth: Natural commutation in AC circuits at zero crossing; forced commutation in DC. Explain class A self-commutation, class B resonant pulse, class C complementary, class D auxiliary, class E external pulse and class F line. Define circuit turn-off time t_c and compare with device turn-off time t_q. Some syllabi call natural commutation line commutation. Keep depth to waveforms and the condition t_c > t_q; do not derive converter circuits.

figure.aria: Commutation splits into natural, with class F line commutation, and forced, with classes A to E for DC circuits.

chapters.example: A capacitor commutation circuit has C = 1 μF charged to 200 V. The load current is 5 A. Find the circuit turn-off time t_c = C V / I. The SCR needs t_q = 30 μs. Is commutation successful? Answer: t_c = 1 μF × 200 V / 5 A = 40 μs; 40 μs > 30 μs, so yes.
chapters.trap: Natural commutation cannot turn off a DC-fed SCR; forced commutation must reverse-bias the SCR for longer than t_q, not just bring current to zero.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 and 1.3 for SCR holding current and turn-on.
chapters.leave: AC voltage controller circuits with TRIAC go to 1.5 and Unit 5; inverter commutation is not repeated here.

chapters.idea: TRIAC and DIAC make a bidirectional AC switch, while GTO is a gate-turn-off thyristor for DC and high-power switching.
chapters.depth: TRIAC structure as two SCRs in antiparallel, MT1, MT2 and gate; four triggering quadrants. DIAC as a bidirectional trigger diode with breakover voltage V_BO. GTO structure, turn-off gain and negative gate pulse. Cover V-I curves and applications. Some syllabi call the TRIAC a bidirectional triode thyristor. Keep gate drive details short; those are in 1.7.

figure.title: TRIAC equivalent
figure.aria: Two SCRs are connected back-to-back between MT2 and MT1; a gate pulse fires one SCR for each half-cycle.

chapters.example: A TRIAC phase controller runs from 230 V rms, 50 Hz with a 100 Ω load. The firing angle is α = 90°. Find the rms load voltage and load power. Use V_rms = V_s sqrt(1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)). Answer: V_rms = 230 × sqrt(0.5) = 162.6 V; P = 162.6²/100 = 264.5 W.
chapters.trap: A TRIAC is not a perfect AC switch: it needs gate current in the correct quadrant, and it can have commutation failure with inductive loads. GTO turn-off needs a large negative gate pulse.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for SCR latching; chapter 1.3 for gate triggering.
chapters.leave: AC voltage controller design and three-phase versions go to Unit 5; GTO gate drive details go to 1.7.

chapters.idea: Power BJT, MOSFET and IGBT are three-terminal controlled switches with different input and output behaviour; the IGBT combines a MOSFET gate with a BJT output.
chapters.depth: BJT: current-controlled, saturation, quasi-saturation, secondary breakdown and safe operating area. MOSFET: voltage-controlled, R_DS(on), body diode, gate charge and Miller plateau. IGBT: MOS gate, bipolar conduction, V_CE(sat), tail current, and no reverse blocking in many devices. Compare static and dynamic characteristics and selection. Some syllabi call the IGBT an insulated-gate bipolar transistor; use the full name once.

figure.title: IGBT equivalent
figure.aria: A gate voltage controls a MOSFET whose output drives the base of a bipolar transistor between collector and emitter.

chapters.example: A power MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 0.1 Ω. An IGBT has V_CE(sat) = 2 V. Compare conduction loss at 5 A and at 50 A. Which device is better at each current? Answer: at 5 A, MOSFET 2.5 W, IGBT 10 W; at 50 A, MOSFET 250 W, IGBT 100 W. Crossover current = 2 V / 0.1 Ω = 20 A.
chapters.trap: MOSFET loss rises as I², IGBT loss rises as I; the crossover current decides the choice. Do not ignore the MOSFET body diode or the IGBT tail current.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for diode curves; basic BJT and MOSFET from electronics.
chapters.leave: Gate driver circuits and snubbers go to 1.7; switching loss and thermal design go to 1.8.

chapters.idea: Ratings and protection decide whether a device survives; snubbers limit dv/dt and di/dt, and gate drives deliver clean pulses.
chapters.depth: Cover voltage, current, surge, di/dt and dv/dt ratings; derating; series and parallel operation. Turn-on snubber (series L) and turn-off snubber (parallel R-C), freewheeling diode. Gate drive: isolation, pulse transformer, optocoupler, gate resistor and negative bias for IGBT. Read absolute maximum ratings, thermal resistance, gate charge and safe operating area. Some syllabi call the R-C snubber a turn-off snubber. Keep design to first-order energy and resistor power; do not repeat converter design.

figure.title: Snubber and gate drive
figure.aria: A gate driver sends pulses to a 400 V switch; a 10 nF capacitor with series resistor is connected across the switch to absorb turn-off energy.

chapters.example: A turn-off snubber has C_s = 10 nF across a switch that blocks 400 V. The switching frequency is 20 kHz. Find the energy stored in C_s at turn-off and the power dissipated in R_s if all that energy is lost each cycle. Answer: E = 0.5 × 10 nF × (400 V)² = 0.8 mJ; P = 0.8 mJ × 20 kHz = 16 W.
chapters.trap: A snubber capacitor does not save energy; it moves loss to the resistor. The resistor must be rated for continuous pulse power, and the snubber must be placed close to the switch.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for SCR ratings; chapter 1.6 for MOSFET and IGBT gate behaviour.
chapters.leave: Detailed thermal resistance and junction temperature go to 1.8; series/parallel operation in converters is in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Switching loss comes from voltage and current overlapping during transitions, and thermal design keeps junction temperature below the limit.
chapters.depth: Define turn-on and turn-off energy with the linear approximation E = 0.5 V I t. Average switching power P_sw = E f_s. Add conduction loss. Thermal path: junction, case, heat sink and ambient; Rθ_JC, Rθ_CS and Rθ_SA; T_j = T_a + P(Rθ_JC + Rθ_CS + Rθ_SA). Introduce transient thermal impedance. Some syllabi call the heat-sink thermal resistance Rθ_SA.

figure.aria: Heat flows from the device junction through the case and heat sink to ambient; each layer adds thermal resistance.

chapters.example: A switch has V = 200 V, I = 10 A, t_on = 1 μs, t_off = 2 μs, f_s = 10 kHz. Use linear switching and find P_sw. The ambient is 40 °C, Rθ_JC = 1.0 °C/W, Rθ_CS = 0.5 °C/W. Find the heat-sink Rθ_SA needed to keep T_j ≤ 125 °C. Answer: P_sw = 0.5 × 200 × 10 × 3 μs × 10 kHz = 30 W; total allowed Rθ = (125 − 40)/30 = 2.833 °C/W; Rθ_SA = 2.833 − 1.5 = 1.33 °C/W.
chapters.trap: Use the total transition time for the energy triangle and remember f_s is per second. Thermal resistances add in series; a lower Rθ_SA means a bigger heat sink.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.7 for snubber energy; chapter 1.6 for device conduction models.
chapters.leave: Converter efficiency and thermal simulation of a full converter go to Unit 3; gate drive loss is not repeated.

chapters.idea: SiC and GaN are wide band-gap semiconductors that switch faster and block higher voltage per unit area than silicon, but they need careful gate drive and layout.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover bandgap (Si 1.1 eV, SiC 3.2 eV, GaN 3.4 eV), critical electric field, thermal conductivity; SiC MOSFET and GaN HEMT; unipolar operation, low Q_g, reverse recovery issues, higher dv/dt and EMI. Compare with Si at 600 V and 1200 V. Read WBG datasheets for gate voltage limits and thermal ratings. Keep it to device-level comparison, not converter design.

figure.aria: Silicon has a bandgap of 1.1 eV and critical field about 0.3 MV/cm; SiC and GaN have wider bandgaps and much higher critical fields.

chapters.example: A SiC MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ. A silicon MOSFET of the same voltage rating has R_DS(on) = 100 mΩ. Both carry 20 A. Find the conduction loss in each and the ratio. State one reason SiC is chosen. Answer: P_SiC = 20² × 0.02 = 8 W; P_Si = 20² × 0.1 = 40 W; ratio 1:5. SiC gives lower loss and can switch at higher frequency.
chapters.trap: Wide band-gap devices are not drop-in replacements: gate voltage limits, negative spikes and EMI from fast dv/dt can destroy them. Do not assume GaN has a simple body diode.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.6 for MOSFET and IGBT behaviour; chapter 1.7 for gate drive.
chapters.leave: Converter topologies for WBG go to Unit 3; EMI standards are outside this unit.
